title: Physiological considerations of the impacts of climate change for marsupials and monotremes
content:
Abstract
Marsupials and monotremes inhabit regions where climate change is impacting environmental temperature, water availability, ecological interactions and extreme environmental events. Here, I evaluate how physiological traits shape species responses to these changes and assess how physiological knowledge can inform conservation. Marsupials and monotremes share the fundamental endothermic bauplan of placental mammals and are not intrinsically physiologically inferior; they are competent endotherms and can exploit heterothermy, behavioural flexibility and physiological plasticity to withstand environmental change. However, species with specialist niches are at particular risk of the consequences of global warming. Arboreal folivores are vulnerable because low evaporative water loss, dietary water dependence and obligate intake of plant secondary metabolites constrain energy, water and thermal balance. Hibernators face increased energetic costs, phenological mismatches and increased predation as warmer winters, reduced snow cover and altered resource availability disrupt seasonal cycles. Diurnal, semi-fossorial, semi-aquatic and refugia-reliant species may also be exposed to conditions beyond their physiological tolerance. Extreme events such as heatwaves, drought, fire and storms can interact with, and exacerbate, ecological variables such as disease, food and shelter availability and predation risk. Physiologically informed conservation that incorporates mechanistic species distribution models, evidence-based translocation, adaptive fire management, provision of supplementary resources, predator control, and disease surveillance and management can improve climate adaptation strategies. While the physiological capacity for Australian marsupials to respond to climate change is comparatively well understood, this review reveals both a paucity of relevant physiological knowledge for marsupials from Melanesia/Wallacea and South America and insufficient integration of physiological knowledge into some management decisions.
